propositions.text: SOCAN initiated a proceeding before the Copyright Board to set royalty rates for 2014–2026 for online audiovisual and user-generated content services.
propositions.quote: The Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada (SOCAN) initiated a proceeding before the Copyright Board seeking an order of the Board establishing the royalty rates (i.e., setting tariffs) SOCAN will collect for 2014–2026 from users of musical works in online audiovisual services and user-generated content services.

propositions.text: The Copyright Board has authority to set such rates under the Copyright Act.
propositions.quote: The Copyright Board has the authority to set such rates under the Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42.

paragraphs.summary: The court states SOCAN initiated a proceeding before the Copyright Board to set royalty rates for 2014–2026, and the Board has authority under the Copyright Act.

propositions.text: The Board divided the proceeding into two phases and identified four preliminary issues for Phase I.
propositions.quote: During case management, the Board decided to divide the proceeding into two phases and identified “four preliminary issues” to be considered in Phase I

propositions.text: The four preliminary issues concern the applicability of CBC v SODRAC, statutory exceptions, interpretation of paragraph 66.501(a), and rights triggered by offline viewing copies.
propositions.quote: 1. Does the Supreme Court’s decision in CBC v SODRAC, 2015 SCC 57, apply to tariff proceedings before the Board? If so, how? 2. Is it possible for the statutory exceptions (listed in the Order) [ss. 29.21, 29.24, 30.7, 30.71 and 31.1 of the Copyright Act] to apply to a class of services covered by the Proposed Tariffs? 3. What is the interpretation of paragraph 66.501(a) of the [the Act]? 4. When offline viewing copies are offered, created, and used, which rights are triggered?

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Board divided the proceeding into two phases and identified four preliminary issues for Phase I concerning legal applicability and interpretation.

propositions.text: The Board included two safeguards in Phase I Notice; the second allows reconsideration if Phase II evidence casts doubt on Phase I conclusions.
propositions.quote: The second of those safeguards, relevant to this matter, was that “if evidence in Phase II significantly throws into doubt a conclusion from Phase I, parties can ask the Board to reconsider that conclusion”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Board included a safeguard allowing reconsideration of Phase I conclusions if Phase II evidence casts doubt.

propositions.text: On November 21, 2025, the Board issued a Phase I Ruling with conclusions on preliminary issues but not final tariff determinations.
propositions.quote: On November 21, 2025, the Board issued a ruling setting out its “conclusions on these preliminary issues” stating the ruling “does not constitute [the Board’s] final determinations on the Proposed Tariffs under consideration”

propositions.text: The Board reminded parties of the safeguard allowing reconsideration if Phase II evidence casts doubt on Phase I conclusions.
propositions.quote: The Board also reminded the parties of its safeguard that “if evidence in Phase II significantly throws into doubt a conclusion from Phase I, parties can ask the Board to reconsider that conclusion”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Board issued a Phase I Ruling with preliminary conclusions and reminded parties of the reconsideration safeguard.

propositions.text: SOCAN filed an application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling.
propositions.quote: SOCAN filed an application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling.

paragraphs.summary: The court states SOCAN filed an application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling.

propositions.text: Three respondents move to strike the application, arguing the Phase I Ruling is interlocutory and not judicially reviewable.
propositions.quote: They contend that the Phase I Ruling is an interlocutory one in a larger and ongoing administrative process and is therefore not a “decision” amenable to judicial review

propositions.text: They argue SOCAN has not exhausted adequate alternative recourse and no exceptional circumstances justify early judicial intervention.
propositions.quote: that even if it were a decision that could be judicially reviewed in principle, SOCAN has not exhausted adequate and effective alternative recourse; and that no exceptional circumstances exist to justify early judicial intervention.

propositions.text: They seek lump sum or heightened costs, arguing SOCAN’s application should never have been brought.
propositions.quote: These respondents seek lump sum costs of $20,000, or costs on a heightened basis, on the ground SOCAN’s application should never have been brought.

paragraphs.summary: The respondents argue the Phase I Ruling is interlocutory and not reviewable, SOCAN has not exhausted remedies, no exceptional circumstances exist, and seek costs.

propositions.text: SOCAN disagrees but says if the motion succeeds, a $5,000 costs award is more appropriate than heightened costs.
propositions.quote: However, it contends that if the respondents’ motion is successful, heightened costs are not justified and that a $5,000 costs award is more appropriate.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN disagrees but says if the motion succeeds, $5,000 costs are more appropriate than heightened costs.

propositions.text: The court would grant the motion to strike and dismiss the judicial review application.
propositions.quote: I would grant the motion to strike and dismiss the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: The court agrees respondents are entitled to costs but $5,000 is appropriate, not heightened costs.
propositions.quote: While I agree the respondents are entitled to costs, I agree with SOCAN that a costs award of $5,000 is more appropriate in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court would grant the motion to strike, dismiss the application, and award $5,000 costs to respondents.

propositions.text: To succeed on a motion to strike, respondents must show the application is clearly improper with no possibility of success.
propositions.quote: the respondents must demonstrate that SOCAN’s application for judicial review is “so clearly improper as to be bereft of any possibility of success”

propositions.text: This is a high threshold, citing JP Morgan and David Bull Laboratories.
propositions.quote: This is admittedly a high threshold to meet.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the high threshold for a motion to strike: application must be clearly improper with no chance of success.

propositions.text: No evidence is admissible on a motion to strike; facts in the notice are presumed true; documents referred to can be considered.
propositions.quote: No evidence is admissible on a motion to strike, and with limited exceptions, we must presume the facts asserted in the notice of application are true; documents referred to in the notice of application or incorporated by reference can be taken into account

propositions.text: Documents include Phase I Notice, Phase I Ruling, and an earlier Board ruling CB-CDA 2025-004.
propositions.quote: Here, those documents include the Phase I Notice and the Phase I Ruling, as well as an earlier Board ruling, CB-CDA 2025-004 dated January 16, 2025.

paragraphs.summary: The court states no evidence is admissible on a motion to strike; facts in the notice are presumed true; relevant documents include Phase I Notice and rulings.

propositions.text: Absent exceptional circumstances, parties must exhaust administrative process before court.
propositions.quote: Absent exceptional circumstances, parties to an administrative process cannot proceed to the court system until that process has run its course

propositions.text: This principle is supported by C.B. Powell and Dugré.
propositions.quote: Canada (Border Services Agency) v. C.B. Powell Limited, 2010 FCA 61 at para. 31 [C.B. Powell]; Dugré v. Canada (Attorney General), 2021 FCA 8 at paras. 34, 37 [Dugré].

paragraphs.summary: The court states parties must exhaust administrative process before court absent exceptional circumstances, citing C.B. Powell and Dugré.

propositions.text: This principle applies to all matters before the administrative decision maker.
propositions.quote: This principle applies “to all matters that arise” before the administrative decision maker

propositions.text: Procedural fairness concerns do not meet the exceptional circumstances threshold, citing Herbert.
propositions.quote: A procedural fairness concern does not meet the “exceptional circumstances” threshold

paragraphs.summary: The court states the exhaustion principle applies to all matters and procedural fairness concerns do not meet exceptional circumstances, citing Herbert.

propositions.text: The rule prevents fragmentation, costs, delays, and waste from premature court proceedings.
propositions.quote: The purpose of this rule is to prevent “fragmentation of the administrative process and piecemeal court proceedings”, to eliminate “the large costs and delays associated with premature forays to court”, and to avoid “the waste associated with hearing an interlocutory judicial review when the applicant for judicial review may succeed at the end of the administrative process anyway”

propositions.text: This is supported by C.B. Powell and Dugré.
propositions.quote: C.B. Powell at para. 32, cited in Dugré at para. 34.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the rule prevents fragmentation, costs, delays, and waste from premature court proceedings, citing C.B. Powell and Dugré.

propositions.text: To bypass administrative process, interlocutory decision consequences must be immediate and radical, threatening rule of law.
propositions.quote: the consequences of an interlocutory decision [must] be so ‘immediate and radical’ that they call into question the rule of law

propositions.text: This is from Dugré quoting Wilson.
propositions.quote: Dugré at para. 35, quoting from Wilson v. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, 2015 FCA 17 at paras. 31–33 [Wilson].

paragraphs.summary: The court states interlocutory decisions must have immediate, radical consequences threatening rule of law to bypass administrative process, citing Dugré and Wilson.

propositions.text: SOCAN seeks to quash Phase I Ruling and declarations on procedural fairness, errors, issue timing, and statutory exceptions.
propositions.quote: SOCAN’s notice of application seeks an order quashing the Phase I Ruling as well as various declarations, including declarations that (i) the Board failed to discharge its duty of procedural fairness by deciding an issue that was outside the scope of Phase I; (ii) the Board erred in fact and law or reached a decision that is unreasonable; (iii) the Board shall not decide certain issues until the completion of Phase II; and (iv) two exceptions in the Copyright Act do not apply in particular circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN seeks to quash the Phase I Ruling and declarations on procedural fairness, errors, issue timing, and statutory exceptions.

propositions.text: The respondents have met the high threshold to strike the application as premature.
propositions.quote: the respondents have persuaded me that that threshold is met here. I find SOCAN’s application for judicial review premature for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondents met the high threshold and SOCAN’s application is premature.

propositions.text: Only administrative actions affecting rights, legal obligations, or causing prejudice are judicially reviewable.
propositions.quote: only administrative action that affects rights, imposes legal obligations, or causes prejudicial effects is amenable to judicial review

propositions.text: This principle is supported by multiple FCA cases including Democracy Watch and Toronto Port Authority.
propositions.quote: Democracy Watch v. Canada (Attorney General), 2020 FCA 69 at para. 19; Tsleil-Waututh Nation v. Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 153 at paras. 175–176, leave to appeal to SCC refused, 38379 (2 May 2019); Democracy Watch v. Canada (Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner), 2009 FCA 15 at para. 10 [Democracy Watch]; Air Canada v. Toronto Port Authority Et Al, 2011 FCA 347 at para. 29 [Toronto Port Authority]; (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Canadian Council for Refugees, 2021 FCA 72 at para. 94 [Canadian Council for Refugees]; Air Passenger Rights v. Canada (Attorney General), 2024 FCA 128 paras. 18–31.

paragraphs.summary: The court states only administrative actions affecting rights or obligations are judicially reviewable, citing multiple FCA cases.

propositions.text: The Phase I Ruling does not affect legal rights or impose obligations warranting judicial review at this stage.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded the Phase I Ruling affects legal rights, imposes legal obligations, or causes prejudicial effects to SOCAN that warrant judicial review at this stage of the proceeding.

propositions.text: Phase I Ruling may affect proceeding conduct but is like many interlocutory orders.
propositions.quote: While I accept that the Phase I Ruling may affect the way the balance of the proceeding to determine the tariffs is conducted, that may be said of many interlocutory orders.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Phase I Ruling does not affect legal rights warranting review and is like many interlocutory orders.

propositions.text: SOCAN argues the Board’s decision is final in substance despite its description and denies manipulation of prematurity doctrine.
propositions.quote: SOCAN posits that the Board’s decision is final in substance no matter how the Board describes it. In doing so, SOCAN says it is not suggesting that the Board intended to manipulate the prematurity doctrine.

propositions.text: SOCAN relies on Federal Court decisions where decision makers tried to shield from judicial review, but circumstances differ here.
propositions.quote: Yet, it relies on Federal Court decisions where the relevant administrative decision maker was seen as trying to shield itself from judicial review: Whalen v. Fort McMurray No. 468 First Nation, 2019 FC 732 at para. 23, and GCT Canada Limited Partnership v. Vancouver Fraser Port Authority, 2020 FC 1062 at para. 44, appeal dismissed, 2021 FCA 183. The circumstances at issue here are simply not comparable to those addressed in those cases.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN argues the Board’s decision is final in substance and relies on cases of shielding from review, but circumstances differ here.

propositions.text: SOCAN submits this Court recognized a first order of the Board in bifurcated proceeding as reviewable.
propositions.quote: SOCAN also submits that this Court has previously recognized a first order of the Board in a bifurcated proceeding as a matter amenable to judicial review.

propositions.text: The court agrees CAIP is distinguishable because the decision disallowed royalties from an entire class, parties consented, and it predates recent cases.
propositions.quote: But I agree with the respondents that Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada v. Canadian Assn. of Internet Providers (C.A.), 2002 FCA 166 [CAIP] is distinguishable. First, the decision under review in CAIP—the Board’s first decision in a bifurcated proceeding—disentitled SOCAN from collecting royalties from an entire class of users and thus was final in that respect: CAIP at paras. 2, 4, 23. Second, the parties consented to the Court’s jurisdiction, and prematurity was not addressed: CAIP at paras. 33–34. Finally, CAIP predates Democracy Watch, Toronto Port Authority, and Canadian Council for Refugees.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN submits this Court recognized a first Board order as reviewable, but the court finds CAIP distinguishable for finality, consent, and timing.

propositions.text: SOCAN's reliance on Wilson is misplaced because Wilson involved bifurcation creating a natural break between phases.
propositions.quote: I also agree with the respondents that SOCAN’s reliance on Wilson is misplaced. In Wilson the administrative decision maker bifurcated the proceeding into a merits and remedy phase—creating a “natural break between two separate phases of the proceedings”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN's reliance on Wilson misplaced because Wilson involved bifurcation creating a natural break between phases.

propositions.text: Here, the Board bifurcated the proceeding but has not applied Phase I Ruling legal interpretations yet.
propositions.quote: In contrast, here the Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties but has yet to apply the legal interpretations set out in its Phase I Ruling.

propositions.text: Phase I and Phase II together concern the merits of the proceeding, not separate phases.
propositions.quote: In other words, Phase I and Phase II together concern the merits of the proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board bifurcated the proceeding but Phase I and II together concern the merits, unlike Wilson.

propositions.text: SOCAN has not exhausted alternative remedies as Phase I Ruling is preliminary and parties can ask for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: SOCAN has not exhausted the available alternative remedies. The Phase I Ruling explicitly expresses its preliminary nature and acknowledges the parties’ right to ask the Board to reconsider a Phase I conclusion if the evidence in Phase II significantly throws that conclusion into doubt.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN has not exhausted alternative remedies since Phase I Ruling is preliminary and reconsideration is possible.

propositions.text: SOCAN alleges Board's safeguard is inadequate because legal questions cannot be doubted by evidence.
propositions.quote: First, insofar as the Phase I Ruling addresses questions of law, they cannot be thrown into doubt by evidence.

propositions.text: SOCAN alleges Board's conclusions will limit evidence tendered in Phase II.
propositions.quote: Second, the Board’s conclusions will limit the evidence that may be tendered in Phase II.

paragraphs.summary: SOCAN alleges Board's safeguard is inadequate because legal questions can't be doubted by evidence and conclusions limit Phase II evidence.

propositions.text: The Board is master of its procedure with broad discretion and powers under Copyright Act and Rules.
propositions.quote: the Board is the master of its own procedure: Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency (Access Copyright) v. Canada, 2018 FCA 58 at para. 171. More specifically, the Board has broad discretion and powers concerning its processes

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board has broad discretion and powers over its procedures under the Copyright Act and Rules.

propositions.text: The Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with parties as part of case management.
propositions.quote: the Board bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with the parties as part of its case management, as it was empowered to do.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board properly bifurcated the proceeding in consultation with parties as part of case management.

propositions.text: SOCAN can raise issues before the Board in case management or Phase II and has not exhausted alternative remedies.
propositions.quote: I see nothing that precludes SOCAN from raising the matters it seeks to raise in its application for judicial review of the Phase I Ruling before the Board

propositions.text: Board has been transparent that Phase I conclusions may be revisited if Phase II evidence throws them into doubt.
propositions.quote: the Board has been consistently transparent with the parties through the Phase I Notice and the Phase I Ruling—Phase I conclusions may be revisited should Phase II evidence significantly throw any one of them into doubt.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN can raise issues before the Board and Board has been transparent about revisiting Phase I conclusions.

propositions.text: No exceptional circumstances justify early court recourse for Phase I Ruling as consequences are not immediate or radical.
propositions.quote: there are no exceptional circumstances that would justify early recourse to the courts in respect of the Phase I Ruling. The consequences of the Phase I Ruling, as an interlocutory one, cannot be described in the terms outlined in Dugré and Wilson

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no exceptional circumstances justify early court recourse for Phase I Ruling as consequences are not immediate or radical.

propositions.text: Even constitutional or jurisdictional questions cannot attract interlocutory relief; circumstances here are not exceptional.
propositions.quote: even constitutional questions or questions qualified as ‘jurisdictional’ questions cannot attract interlocutory relief

propositions.text: The circumstances here are not exceptional to justify interlocutory relief.
propositions.quote: The same must be said here—the circumstances are not exceptional.

paragraphs.summary: The court states constitutional or jurisdictional questions cannot get interlocutory relief and finds circumstances here are not exceptional.

propositions.text: SOCAN may succeed at Phase II or later raise same challenges by judicial review.
propositions.quote: at the end of Phase II, SOCAN may succeed in obtaining the tariffs it seeks

propositions.text: SOCAN is not precluded from raising current issues in judicial review after Phase II decision.
propositions.quote: SOCAN is not precluded from raising the matters raised in its current application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN may succeed at Phase II or later raise same challenges by judicial review.

propositions.text: SOCAN should raise issues before the Board or risk court not considering them later.
propositions.quote: If it does not, but could have, it risks this Court exercising its discretion to not consider the issue on a subsequent application for judicial review

propositions.text: Court ordinarily will not consider judicial review arguments not made before administrative decision-maker.
propositions.quote: This Court will ordinarily not consider on judicial review an argument that was not made before the administrative decision-maker.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds SOCAN should raise issues before the Board or risk court not considering them later, citing precedent.

propositions.text: Motion to strike is granted and judicial review application dismissed without prejudice to Phase II review.
propositions.quote: I would grant the motion to strike and dismiss the application for judicial review. And, while it should be clear from these reasons, I reiterate that if SOCAN decides, upon completion of the administrative process, to seek judicial review of the Phase II decision, this dismissal is without prejudice

paragraphs.summary: The court grants the motion to strike and dismisses the judicial review application without prejudice to Phase II review.

propositions.text: Costs awarded to three respondents in lump sum of $5,000.
propositions.quote: I would award costs to the three respondents in the lump sum all-inclusive amount of $5,000.

paragraphs.summary: The court awards costs to three respondents in lump sum of $5,000.
